title: Geometrical and Optical Isomerism
topicTitle: Concept of geometrical isomerism (cis and trans) and optical isomerism (d and l form)
notes: **Geometrical Isomerism (Cis-Trans Isomerism):** Arises due to **restricted rotation** around a carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) or in cyclic systems. Two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon can be arranged on the same side (**cis**, Z) or opposite sides (**trans**, E). Requirement: (1) Restricted rotation (double bond or ring), (2) Each doubly bonded carbon must have two different substituents. If either carbon has two identical groups, geometrical isomerism is impossible.

**Cis-Trans Nomenclature:** **Cis** (Latin: on this side) — similar/higher priority groups on the same side of the double bond. **Trans** (Latin: across) — similar/higher priority groups on opposite sides. For but-2-ene: cis-but-2-ene has both $CH_3$ groups on same side; trans-but-2-ene has them opposite. Cis isomer has net dipole moment; trans isomer usually has zero dipole moment (symmetrical).

**E-Z Nomenclature (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog Rules):** Used when substituents are not simply 'same/different'. Assign priority to each substituent on a double-bonded carbon using **atomic number** (higher Z = higher priority). If higher priority groups are on the **same side** → **Z** (Zusammen = together). If on **opposite sides** → **E** (Entgegen = opposite). For but-2-ene: both carbons have $CH_3$ (priority) > H. Cis = Z, Trans = E. For 1-bromo-1-chloro-2-fluoroethene: priorities Br > Cl on C1, F > H on C2.

**Physical Properties — Cis vs Trans:** **Boiling Point:** Cis > Trans (cis has net dipole → stronger intermolecular forces). But-2-ene: cis BP 3.7°C, trans BP 0.9°C. **Melting Point:** Trans > Cis (trans packs better in crystal lattice). But-2-ene: cis MP -138.9°C, trans MP -105.5°C. **Density:** Cis > Trans. **Solubility:** Cis > Trans in polar solvents (dipole moment). **Stability:** Trans > Cis (less steric strain). Heat of hydrogenation: cis-but-2-ene = -119 kJ/mol, trans-but-2-ene = -115 kJ/mol (trans more stable by ~4 kJ/mol).

**Geometrical Isomerism in Cyclic Systems:** In rings, restricted rotation is due to the ring structure. **Cis**: both substituents on same face of ring (both up or both down). **Trans**: substituents on opposite faces. For 1,2-disubstituted cyclopropane/cyclobutane/cyclopentane/cyclohexane. In cyclohexane chair conformation: cis-1,2 can be both axial/equatorial (diaxial or diequatorial); trans-1,2 must be one axial, one equatorial. Stability: diequatorial > axial-equatorial > diaxial.

**Conditions for Optical Isomerism (Chirality):** A molecule is **chiral** (optically active) if it lacks an **improper axis of symmetry** (no plane of symmetry, no center of symmetry, no alternating axis of symmetry). Simplest criterion: presence of a **chiral center (stereogenic center)** — typically a carbon with **four different substituents** ($sp^3$ hybridized). Such a carbon is called an **asymmetric carbon** or **chiral carbon**.

**Enantiomers (d- and l-forms):** A chiral molecule exists as two non-superimposable mirror images called **enantiomers**. **d-form (dextrorotatory, +):** rotates plane-polarized light **clockwise** (to the right). **l-form (levorotatory, -):** rotates plane-polarized light **anticlockwise** (to the left). The prefixes d- and l- (or + and -) refer **only to optical rotation direction**, NOT to absolute configuration (R/S). Example: (+)-lactic acid (d-lactic acid) and (-)-lactic acid (l-lactic acid).

**Racemic Mixture (Racemate):** An **equimolar mixture** of d- and l-enantiomers. Net optical rotation = **zero** (rotations cancel). Denoted as **dl-** or **(±)-**. Example: (±)-lactic acid. Racemic mixtures have different physical properties (MP, BP, solubility) from pure enantiomers. **Racemization:** conversion of enantiomerically pure compound to racemic mixture (e.g., by heat, light, acid/base catalysis via carbocation or enolate intermediate).

**Resolution of Racemic Mixture:** Separation of enantiomers. Methods: (1) **Mechanical separation** — only for crystals with distinct shapes (Pasteur's method for sodium ammonium tartrate). (2) **Biochemical method** — enzymes/microorganisms selectively react with one enantiomer. (3) **Chromatography** — chiral stationary phase (HPLC, GC). (4) **Diastereomeric salt formation** — react with a **chiral resolving agent** (e.g., (+)-tartaric acid, brucine) to form diastereomeric salts with different solubilities, separate by fractional crystallization, then regenerate enantiomers.

**Diastereomers:** Stereoisomers that are **NOT mirror images** of each other. Occur when a molecule has **two or more chiral centers**. For n chiral centers, max $2^n$ stereoisomers ( $2^{n-1}$ pairs of enantiomers). Diastereomers have **different physical and chemical properties** (MP, BP, solubility, reactivity) and can be separated by ordinary methods (distillation, crystallization, chromatography). Example: Tartaric acid has 2 chiral centers → 3 stereoisomers: (+)-, (-)-, and meso-tartaric acid.

**Meso Compounds:** Molecules with **multiple chiral centers** but an **internal plane of symmetry**, making them **optically inactive** overall. The chiral centers have opposite configurations (R,S) that cancel rotation. Example: **meso-Tartaric acid** (2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid) — has plane of symmetry through C2-C3 bond. Meso compounds are **achiral despite having chiral centers**. They are diastereomers of the enantiomeric pair.

**D-L System (Fischer Convention) vs d-l System:** **D-L** (capital) refers to **absolute configuration** relative to glyceraldehyde. **D-glyceraldehyde** = (R)-2,3-dihydroxypropanal (historically assigned). **L-glyceraldehyde** = (S)-2,3-dihydroxypropanal. For sugars/amino acids: D/L denotes configuration at the **highest-numbered chiral carbon** (penultimate carbon). **d-l** (lowercase) refers to **optical rotation direction** (+/-). **No correlation between D/L and d/l!** D-glucose is d-(+); D-fructose is l-(-).

**R-S System (Cahn-Ingold-Prelog Absolute Configuration):** Unambiguous designation of absolute configuration at a chiral center. Rules: (1) Assign priority 1-4 by atomic number (higher Z = higher priority). (2) Orient molecule so lowest priority (4) points away. (3) Trace 1\u21922\u21923: clockwise = **R** (Rectus), anticlockwise = **S** (Sinister). For double-bonded atoms: duplicate the atom (C=O treated as C bonded to O, O, phantom). Example: Lactic acid: OH(1) > COOH(2) > CH3(3) > H(4). If H is back and 1\u21922\u21923 is clockwise \u2192 R.

**Optical Activity — Specific Rotation:** Measured using a **polarimeter**. **Specific rotation** $[\alpha]_D^T = \frac{\alpha}{l \times c}$ where $\alpha$ = observed rotation (degrees), $l$ = path length (dm), $c$ = concentration (g/mL for solutions, g/100mL for pure liquids). $D$ = sodium D-line (589 nm), $T$ = temperature (°C). Units: deg\u00b7mL\u00b7g\u207b\u00b9\u00b7dm\u207b\u00b9. Enantiomers have equal magnitude, opposite sign. Racemic mixture: $[\alpha] = 0$.

**Optical Purity and Enantiomeric Excess (ee):** **Enantiomeric excess** $ee = \frac{[R] - [S]}{[R] + [S]} \times 100\% = \frac{\text{observed } [\alpha]}{\text{pure enantiomer } [\alpha]} \times 100\%$. **Optical purity** = ee. If a sample has $[\alpha] = +10\degree$ and pure enantiomer has $[\alpha] = +20\degree$, then ee = 50% (75% R, 25% S). Pharmaceutical synthesis targets ee > 99% (often > 99.9%) for single-enantiomer drugs.

**Importance in Biology and Medicine:** **Enzymes/receptors are chiral** — they distinguish enantiomers. **Thalidomide tragedy (1960s):** (R)-thalidomide = sedative; (S)-thalidomide = teratogenic (birth defects). In vivo racemization occurs. **Ibuprofen:** (S)-enantiomer is active; (R)-enantiomer converts to (S) in body. **L-DOPA** (L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) treats Parkinson's; D-DOPA is inactive. **Amino acids:** All proteinogenic amino acids are L-configuration (except glycine, achiral). **Sugars:** D-sugars predominate in biology.

**Industrial Production of Enantiopure Compounds:** (1) **Chiral pool synthesis** — start from natural chiral building blocks (amino acids, sugars, terpenes). (2) **Asymmetric synthesis** — chiral catalysts (Noyori hydrogenation, Sharpless epoxidation, Jacobsen epoxidation — Nobel Prizes 2001, 2001, 2021). (3) **Biocatalysis** — engineered enzymes (transaminases, ketoreductases) for high ee. (4) **Chiral resolution** — classical (diastereomeric salts) or simulated moving bed chromatography. (5) **Chiral switches** — re-developing racemic drugs as single enantiomers (esomeprazole from omeprazole, levocetirizine from cetirizine).
confusion: ❌ Confusion: Thinking cis-trans isomerism is possible in but-1-ene ($CH_2=CHCH_2CH_3$) ✅ Correction: **Cis-trans requires EACH double-bonded carbon to have two different groups.** In but-1-ene, C-1 has two H atoms (identical) → no geometrical isomerism possible. Only but-2-ene (and higher internal alkenes) show cis-trans.

❌ Confusion: Believing cis isomer is always more stable than trans ✅ Correction: **Trans is more stable** (lower heat of hydrogenation) due to less steric repulsion between bulky groups on opposite sides. Cis has higher energy. Exception: In small rings (cyclopropene, cyclobutene), cis is forced and trans is impossible/strained.

❌ Confusion: Assuming d- and l- correspond to D- and L- configurations ✅ Correction: **d/l (lowercase) = direction of optical rotation (+/-). D/L (uppercase) = absolute configuration relative to glyceraldehyde.** They are independent! D-glyceraldehyde is d-(+) but D-lactic acid is l-(-). Never assume correlation.

❌ Confusion: Thinking a racemic mixture is 'inactive' because it has no chiral centers ✅ Correction: A racemic mixture CONTAINS chiral molecules (equal amounts of both enantiomers). The mixture is **optically inactive** (net rotation = 0) due to cancellation, not absence of chirality. Each enantiomer is still chiral.

❌ Confusion: Believing meso compounds have no chiral centers ✅ Correction: Meso compounds **DO have chiral centers** (two or more), but they possess an **internal plane of symmetry** that makes the molecule overall achiral. The chiral centers are of opposite configuration (R,S) and their rotations cancel internally.

❌ Confusion: Thinking all compounds with chiral centers are optically active ✅ Correction: **Meso compounds** and **racemic mixtures** are optically inactive despite containing chiral centers. Only **enantiomerically pure** (or enantiomerically enriched) chiral compounds show optical activity.

❌ Confusion: Using 'optical isomerism' and 'geometrical isomerism' interchangeably ✅ Correction: They are **different types of stereoisomerism**. Geometrical isomerism = cis/trans (E/Z) due to restricted rotation (C=C or ring). Optical isomerism = enantiomers/diastereomers due to chirality (asymmetric centers). A molecule can show BOTH (e.g., 3-methylpent-2-ene has E/Z and a chiral center at C-3).
practice:
**Problem 1:** Draw all geometrical isomers of but-2-ene and 1,2-dichlorocyclopropane. Label each as cis/trans and E/Z.

**Solution:**
**But-2-ene ($CH_3CH=CHCH_3$):**
- Each C has CH3 and H. Priority: CH3 > H (C atomic no. 6 > H 1).
- **Cis (Z):** Both CH3 on same side. Dipole moment \u2260 0. BP 3.7\u00b0C.
- **Trans (E):** CH3 groups opposite. Dipole moment = 0. BP 0.9\u00b0C.

**1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane:**
- Ring creates restricted rotation. Two chiral centers.
- **Cis:** Both Cl on same face (both wedges or both dashes). Has plane of symmetry \u2192 **meso compound**, optically inactive.
- **Trans:** Cl on opposite faces (one wedge, one dash). No symmetry \u2192 **chiral**, exists as enantiomeric pair (R,R and S,S).

**Answer:** But-2-ene: cis-(Z) and trans-(E). 1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane: cis-meso, trans-(R,R)/(S,S) enantiomeric pair.

**Problem 2:** A compound with formula $C_4H_8Cl_2$ has two chiral centers and exists as three stereoisomers. Identify the structure and explain.

**Solution:**
1. $C_4H_8Cl_2$ with two chiral centers \u2192 likely 2,3-dichlorobutane ($CH_3CHClCHClCH_3$).
2. Two chiral centers (C-2 and C-3) \u2192 max $2^2 = 4$ stereoisomers.
3. Only 3 stereoisomers exist \u2192 one must be **meso** (internally compensated).
4. The four theoretical: (2R,3R), (2S,3S) = enantiomeric pair; (2R,3S), (2S,3R).
5. (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are identical (meso) due to plane of symmetry through C2-C3 bond.
6. Three stereoisomers: **(+)-2,3-dichlorobutane (2R,3R)**, **(-)-2,3-dichlorobutane (2S,3S)**, **meso-2,3-dichlorobutane (2R,3S)**.

**Answer:** 2,3-Dichlorobutane. Three stereoisomers: one enantiomeric pair + one meso form.

**Problem 3:** Calculate the specific rotation of a mixture containing 8 g of (+)-lactic acid ($[\alpha]_D = +3.8\degree$) and 2 g of (-)-lactic acid ($[\alpha]_D = -3.8\degree$) dissolved in 100 mL water, measured in a 1 dm tube.

**Solution:**
1. Total mass = 10 g in 100 mL \u2192 concentration $c = 10/100 = 0.1$ g/mL.
2. Path length $l = 1$ dm.
3. Enantiomeric excess: mass of (+) = 8 g, mass of (-) = 2 g. Net excess of (+) = 6 g.
4. $ee = (6/10) \times 100\% = 60\%$.
5. Observed rotation $\alpha = ee \times [\alpha]_{pure} = 0.60 \times (+3.8\degree) = +2.28\degree$.
   (Alternatively: $\alpha = [\alpha] \times l \times c_{net}$ where $c_{net}$ = conc. of excess enantiomer = 6g/100mL = 0.06 g/mL. $\alpha = 3.8 \times 1 \times 0.06 = +0.228\degree$? Wait — specific rotation formula: $[\alpha] = \alpha/(l \times c)$. For mixture, observed $\alpha = [\alpha]_{mix} \times l \times c_{total}$. $[\alpha]_{mix} = ee \times [\alpha]_{pure} = 0.6 \times 3.8 = 2.28$. Then $\alpha = 2.28 \times 1 \times 0.1 = 0.228\degree$. But question asks for specific rotation of mixture.
6. Specific rotation of mixture $[\alpha]_{mix} = ee \times [\alpha]_{pure} = 0.60 \times (+3.8) = +2.28\degree$.

**Answer:** Specific rotation of mixture = **+2.28\u00b0** (or $+2.3\u00b0$). Enantiomeric excess = 60%.

**Problem 4:** An organic compound $C_5H_{10}O$ shows geometrical isomerism and has a chiral center. Draw its structure and name all stereoisomers.

**Solution:**
1. $C_5H_{10}O$: DBE = 5 - 10/2 + 1 = 1. One DBE \u2192 could be C=C or ring + OH/aldehyde/ketone.
2. Needs geometrical isomerism \u2192 C=C with two different groups on each carbon.
3. Needs chiral center \u2192 $sp^3$ carbon with 4 different groups.
4. Candidate: **Pent-3-en-2-ol** ($CH_3CH=CHCH(OH)CH_3$).
   - C=C at C-3/C-4: C-3 has H and CH3; C-4 has H and CH(OH)CH3. Two different groups on each \u2192 **E/Z isomerism**.
   - C-2 (CH(OH)CH3) has H, OH, CH3, CH=CHCH3 \u2192 **four different groups** \u2192 chiral center.
5. Stereoisomers: 2 (E/Z) \u00d7 2 (R/S at C-2) = **4 stereoisomers**.
   - (3E,2R)-pent-3-en-2-ol
   - (3E,2S)-pent-3-en-2-ol
   - (3Z,2R)-pent-3-en-2-ol
   - (3Z,2S)-pent-3-en-2-ol
6. (E,2R) and (E,2S) are enantiomers. (Z,2R) and (Z,2S) are enantiomers. Cross pairs are diastereomers.

**Answer:** Pent-3-en-2-ol. Four stereoisomers: (E,R), (E,S), (Z,R), (Z,S). Two enantiomeric pairs.

**Problem 5:** 2.5 g of a chiral compound was dissolved in 50 mL solvent and placed in a 2 dm polarimeter tube. The observed rotation was +0.75\u00b0. The pure enantiomer has $[\alpha]_D = +15.0\u00b0$. Calculate the enantiomeric excess and the mass of each enantiomer in the sample.

**Solution:**
1. Concentration $c = 2.5 / 50 = 0.05$ g/mL.
2. Path length $l = 2$ dm.
3. Observed rotation $\alpha = +0.75\u00b0$.
4. Specific rotation of sample: $[\alpha]_{sample} = \frac{\alpha}{l \times c} = \frac{0.75}{2 \times 0.05} = \frac{0.75}{0.1} = +7.5\u00b0$.
5. Enantiomeric excess: $ee = \frac{[\alpha]_{sample}}{[\alpha]_{pure}} \times 100 = \frac{7.5}{15.0} \times 100 = 50\%$.
6. Let $x$ = mass of major enantiomer, $y$ = mass of minor. $x + y = 2.5$, $x - y = ee \times 2.5 = 1.25$.
7. Solving: $2x = 3.75 \Rightarrow x = 1.875$ g. $y = 2.5 - 1.875 = 0.625$ g.

**Answer:** Enantiomeric excess = 50%. Major enantiomer = 1.875 g, minor enantiomer = 0.625 g.

**Problem 6:** Which of the following show optical isomerism? Explain.
(a) 2-Chlorobutane  (b) 1-Chlorobutane  (c) 2,3-Dichlorobutane  (d) 1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane

**Solution:**
(a) **2-Chlorobutane ($CH_3CHClCH_2CH_3$):** C-2 has H, Cl, CH3, CH2CH3 \u2192 **four different groups** \u2192 **chiral** \u2192 shows optical isomerism (enantiomers).

(b) **1-Chlorobutane ($CH_2ClCH_2CH_2CH_3$):** C-1 has two H atoms (CH2Cl) \u2192 **not a chiral center**. No other chiral centers \u2192 **achiral** \u2192 no optical isomerism.

(c) **2,3-Dichlorobutane ($CH_3CHClCHClCH_3$):** Two chiral centers (C-2, C-3). Exists as **three stereoisomers**: (2R,3R) and (2S,3S) = enantiomeric pair (optically active); meso-(2R,3S) = optically inactive. **Shows optical isomerism** (the enantiomeric pair).

(d) **1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane:** Two chiral centers. **Cis isomer** = meso (plane of symmetry) \u2192 optically inactive. **Trans isomer** = no symmetry \u2192 chiral, exists as enantiomeric pair (1R,2R) and (1S,2S) \u2192 **shows optical isomerism**.

**Answer:** (a) Yes, (b) No, (c) Yes (enantiomeric pair), (d) Yes (trans enantiomers only).
universalFacts: The **first resolution of enantiomers** was performed by **Louis Pasteur in 1848** at age 25. He manually separated left- and right-handed crystals of sodium ammonium tartrate with tweezers under a microscope, proving molecular chirality. This founded stereochemistry.

Over **50% of modern drugs** are chiral, and ~90% of new chiral drugs are marketed as single enantiomers. The 'chiral switch' strategy (re-developing racemic drugs as single enantiomers) has created blockbusters: esomeprazole (Nexium, $6B/yr), levocetirizine (Xyzal), dexlansoprazole.

Life uses **exclusively L-amino acids** and **D-sugars**. The origin is unknown — hypotheses include: circularly polarized light from neutron stars, weak nuclear force parity violation (tiny energy difference ~10\u207b\u00b9\u2077 kT), autocatalytic amplification, or chance in a 'RNA world'. This is one of science's great unsolved mysteries.

**Specific rotation** is the standard quality control for sugar purity in the sugar industry. Sucrose: $[\alpha]_D = +66.5\u00b0$. Glucose: $+52.7\u00b0$. Fructose: $-92.4\u00b0$. **Invert sugar** (hydrolyzed sucrose) has negative rotation due to excess fructose. 'Inversion' = change in sign of rotation. Polarimeters on production lines monitor this in real-time.

The **thalidomide tragedy** transformed drug regulation. Marketed as racemic sedative (1957-1961), caused >10,000 birth defects. The (S)-enantiomer is teratogenic; (R)-enantiomer is therapeutic. But in vivo, they **interconvert** (racemize at chiral center via enolization). Modern FDA requires **enantiomeric purity data** and **chiral toxicology** for all new chiral drugs.
